name: WebAssembly (threads, SIMD, memory limits)
plain: Runs compiled code at near native speed inside the page, with up to 4 GB of memory (16 GB with memory64 in Chrome).
meaning: A site can run heavy code (games, codecs, Photoshop-class tools) with no install. The same speed makes in-browser miners and side channel timing code practical.

access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: No iframe flag; CSP script-src needs 'wasm-unsafe-eval' to compile

limits.headline: Can run fast compiled code inside the page, within memory limits
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads, such as a game, editor or video tool.
can: Run apps made in languages like C++ or Rust inside the page
Use up to 4 GB of memory per page; Chrome can go to 16 GB with memory64
Use several threads at once when the site is isolated
cannot: Skip the browser's rules for web code; it runs in the same safe sandbox
Reach your files, camera or other apps on its own
Use more memory than the limit the browser sets
Run after you close the page

story.what_it_is: A page can run big, compiled programs in your browser at near desktop speed.

marketing.name: WebAssembly
marketing.pitch: The WebAssembly site pitches it as a fast, safe binary format that runs in browsers next to JavaScript.

story.for_you: You open a web app and it feels like a desktop program. Photoshop or a 3D game loads in a tab without an install.
story.for_makers: Makers can bring huge existing programs to the web without rewriting them. This is how big games, CAD and design tools reach anyone with a link.

use_cases.example: Figma runs its design engine as WebAssembly so large files stay smooth.
Unity and Unreal games run in a tab, and Doom style ports run at full speed.
A web conferencing client uses it to compress and clean video and audio.
AutoCAD and Google Earth run in a browser tab using compiled code.
Attackers can hide crypto miners or obfuscated code in compiled form, harder to inspect.
Developers run Python or full databases in the browser with no server.

technical_bounds: wasm32 memory max 65536 pages = 4 GiB per memory in Chrome and Firefox; Safari and mobile browsers often cap lower (about 1 to 2 GiB in practice)
memory64 raises the limit to 16 GiB in V8 (Chrome 133, Firefox 134); real allocations still fail when RAM is short
Threads need SharedArrayBuffer and cross-origin isolation (COOP and COEP)
SIMD: Chrome 91, Firefox 89, Safari 16.4; also tail calls (Chrome 112), GC (Chrome 119, Firefox 120, Safari 18.2)
Under a CSP without 'wasm-unsafe-eval', compile is blocked (Chrome 97)
Sandbox: no direct OS access, only imports provided by JavaScript
